laws.historical_context: The Lebanese Commercial Code of 1942 was enacted during the French Mandate period, replacing Ottoman commercial laws. It was modeled after the French Commercial Code and established the foundation for modern commercial regulation in Lebanon. The Code covers trade acts, merchants, commercial companies, commercial papers (bills of exchange, cheques, promissory notes), and bankruptcy procedures.

It replaced earlier company regulations and aligned Lebanese company law with international standards.

laws.historical_context: The Banking Secrecy Law of 1956 was championed by Finance Minister Raymond Eddé and established Lebanon as the 'Switzerland of the Middle East.' It guaranteed clients complete confidentiality regarding their bank accounts and financial information. The law was a strategic response to regional instability and helped Lebanon build a thriving banking sector attracting billions in Arab and foreign capital. At its peak, Lebanon's banking sector held USD 180 billion in deposits (nearly four times Lebanon's GDP). The 2025 amendment marked a significant shift, removing core elements of banking secrecy to comply with IMF requirements and international anti-corruption standards.

laws.historical_context: The Commercial Register provisions are contained within the Lebanese Commercial Code of 1942. The register serves as a public record of all commercial establishments operating in Lebanon, divided into a general register for traders and companies, and a special register for commercial establishments and contracts. Registration is maintained at each Court of First Instance.

laws.historical_context: Lebanon does not have a standalone Bankruptcy Law. Bankruptcy and insolvency are governed by Book V of the Commercial Code (Articles 459-668) and the Penal Code. The law provides for both voluntary and judicial liquidation, as well as debt restructuring options for distressed businesses. Workers may resort to the Labor Court and the National Social Security Fund to recover pay and benefits from bankrupt firms. The law criminalizes fraudulent bankruptcy.

laws.historical_context: Lebanese maritime law is primarily regulated by the 1947 Maritime Commerce Law (Code de Commerce Maritime) and the Lebanese Commercial Code. Inspired by French maritime law, it contains detailed provisions on ship registration, maritime transport contracts, crew employment, maritime accidents, marine insurance, and arbitration procedures. Lebanon follows international standards including MLC 2006, STCW, SOLAS, and MARPOL conventions.

Foreign companies operating through agents in Lebanon must comply with registration requirements. Agency agreements should clearly define the scope of authority, territory, and compensation terms.

laws.historical_context: The Consumer Protection Law (659/2005) establishes protections for consumers in Lebanon, prohibiting unfair commercial practices. The law was updated by Law 81/2018 on Electronic Transactions to include e-commerce consumer protection provisions. The Ministry of Economy and Trade is responsible for enforcement and publishes monthly consumer protection reports.

laws.historical_context: Lebanon's competition law is primarily governed by Law No. 369 of 2001 on the Protection of Competition. This law aims to promote and protect competition by prohibiting anti-competitive agreements, abuse of dominant positions, and other unfair market practices. Lebanon currently does not have a specialized competition authority; enforcement is mainly through the judiciary, where courts assess competition cases brought by the Ministry of Economy and Trade or private parties. Lebanon was the last country in the Middle East to introduce competition legislation (2022 according to some sources).

laws.historical_context: Lebanon's intellectual property framework is based on Resolution 2385 of 1924 (governing commercial and industrial property) which was amended by the Law of January 31, 1946. Copyright is protected under Law 75/99, and patents under Law 240/2000. Lebanon is compliant with TRIPS standards and has ratified the Paris Convention, Madrid Agreement, and Berne Convention. In 2024, Law 324 reduced trademark protection duration from 15 to 10 years for new registrations. The Ministry of Economy and Trade's Intellectual Property Protection Office (IPPO) oversees IP matters.

laws.historical_context: Law 81/2018 was enacted to address the growing reliance on electronic documents, digital signatures, and online transactions. It provides a comprehensive legal framework for electronic transactions, personal data protection, and associated activities. The law grants electronic documents and signatures the same legal standing as traditional paper-based documents, facilitates e-commerce, and establishes data protection standards. COLIBAC (Lebanese Accreditation Council) oversees electronic authentication services.

laws.historical_context: The Code of Money and Credit is the main regulation of the banking and financial system in Lebanon. It covers the regulation of money, the Central Bank of Lebanon's role and functions, banks' activities, and the activities of professions linked to the banking profession. Law 28/67 amended the Code and established the Higher Banking Commission and the Banking Control Commission at the Central Bank.

laws.historical_context: Law 318/2001 was enacted to combat money laundering and terrorist financing in Lebanon. It established the Special Investigation Commission (SIC) as the sole authority empowered to lift banking secrecy for investigations related to money laundering and terrorist financing. The law was amended by Law 44/2015 to strengthen provisions.
